The closest 2024–2025 work supports controlled activation patching, but does not establish a GRU4Rec-specific diagnostic recipe. [Heimersheim and Nanda (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255) emphasize clean/corrupted activation swaps, complementary restoration and disruption experiments, and sensitivity to metric choice. [Zhang and Nanda (ICLR 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042) show that corruption methods can change localization conclusions; realistic replacements and target-versus-competitor logit differences are useful starting points. [AAAI 2025 research](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/34969) examines interpretability transfer to recurrent architectures, but studies Mamba/RWKV rather than recommendation GRUs.

A proposed adaptation: freeze the existing GRU; construct equal-length histories differing at one historical interaction while preserving the suffix; patch hidden states at successive positions, then recompute the remaining recurrence. Compare restoration/disruption of a fixed target–competitor score margin against self-patches, matched donor histories, and equal-magnitude random-direction interventions. Record hidden-state difference norms alongside margin changes. For a linear readout, Δmargin = (w_target − w_competitor)ᵀΔh exactly; persistent state differences with weak margin effects suggest readout insensitivity along those directions, whereas shrinking differences suggest dynamical attenuation. Older [gating theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00025) connects GRU gates to slow modes and Jacobian dynamics: gate saturation alone therefore cannot establish forgetting. Small gate-logit perturbations or donor-gate patches can test specific hypotheses, using the implementation’s actual gate convention. These are conditional mechanisms of one frozen model, not evidence of user intent or improved generalization; no additional predictor is required.
